title: Velocity and Acceleration in Uniform Circular Motion
statement:
A particle moves around a circle at a constant angular frequency $$\omega$$ (radians per unit time), so if the circle has radius $$r,$$ the particle's speed is $$v = \omega r.$$ The animation below shows the particle along with its __position vector__ $$\vec{r},$$ drawn from the center of the circle. The goal of this problem is to find the particle's acceleration without calculus, by thinking about rotating vectors.

__(a)__ The particle never speeds up or slows down, and its angular velocity never changes. Explain why the particle nevertheless has a nonzero acceleration, and state which direction the velocity vector $$\vec{v}$$ points.

__(b)__ A vector can be drawn starting anywhere, so imagine drawing a copy of $$\vec{v}$$ that always starts at the center of the circle, as in the animation below. Describe what this copied vector does as time goes on, and explain why it is exactly the position vector rotated by $$90^\circ$$ in the direction of the particle's motion and scaled in length by the factor $$\omega.$$

__(c)__ Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, just as velocity is the rate of change of position. Use part (b) to find the acceleration vector $$\vec{a}$$ in terms of $$\omega$$ and $$\vec{r},$$ then rewrite its magnitude in terms of the speed $$v$$ and the radius $$r.$$ Which way does $$\vec{a}$$ point? (The notation $$\hat{r} = \vec{r}/r,$$ pronounced "$$r$$ hat," means a __unit vector__ — a vector of magnitude $$1$$ — in the direction of $$\vec{r}.$$)

__(d)__ In deep space, a ball on the end of a string is swung in a circle, making one revolution in time $$\tau.$$ The free-body diagram is shown below: the only force on the ball is the string tension $$T,$$ pointing toward the center. If the tension is doubled and the ball continues to move in a circle of the same radius, how long does a single revolution take?
answer: (c) $$\vec{a} = -\omega^2\vec{r} = -\dfrac{v^2}{r}\hat{r},$$ pointing toward the center, with magnitude $$a = \omega^2 r = \dfrac{v^2}{r}$$; (d) $$\dfrac{\tau}{\sqrt{2}}$$
solution:
__(a)__ Velocity is a vector: it has a magnitude and a direction. Acceleration occurs whenever the velocity changes, and that can happen because the magnitude changes, because the direction changes, or both. Here the magnitude is constant but the direction changes continuously, so the velocity is changing and the acceleration is nonzero. The velocity points tangent to the circle, in the direction of motion.

__(b)__ The copied velocity vector has constant length (the speed $$\omega r$$ never changes) and its direction rotates steadily, so it sweeps around a circle at the same angular frequency $$\omega$$ as the position vector. Since the velocity is tangent to the circle while the position vector is radial, the velocity is always $$90^\circ$$ ahead of the position vector, rotated in the direction of motion. Its length is the speed, $$\omega r$$ — exactly $$\omega$$ times the length of the position vector. So the velocity vector is the position vector rotated $$90^\circ$$ and scaled by $$\omega.$$

__(c)__ The velocity vector is itself a vector of constant length rotating at angular frequency $$\omega,$$ so the same rule applies again: the acceleration is the velocity vector rotated $$90^\circ$$ and scaled by $$\omega.$$ Two $$90^\circ$$ rotations make $$180^\circ,$$ so $$\vec{a}$$ points opposite the position vector, and the magnitude is scaled by $$\omega$$ twice: $$\vec{a} = -\omega^2\vec{r}.$$ Substituting $$\omega = v/r$$ gives $$a = \omega^2 r = \dfrac{v^2}{r},$$ or in vector form $$\vec{a} = -\dfrac{v^2}{r}\hat{r}.$$ The minus sign says the acceleration points toward the center of the circle.

__(d)__ Newton's second law along the string gives $$T = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}.$$ With $$m$$ and $$r$$ fixed, doubling $$T$$ doubles $$v^2,$$ so $$v$$ is multiplied by $$\sqrt{2}.$$ The period is the circumference over the speed, $$\dfrac{2\pi r}{v},$$ so it shrinks by the same factor: the new period is $$\dfrac{\tau}{\sqrt{2}}.$$

title: Where Gravity Cancels Between the Earth and the Moon
statement:
__Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation__ says that two objects with masses $$m_1$$ and $$m_2,$$ separated by a distance $$r,$$ attract each other with a force of magnitude $$F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2},$$ where $$G \approx 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2}$$ is the gravitational constant. In vector form, $$\vec{F}_{12} = -\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}\hat{r}_{12},$$ where $$\hat{r}_{12}$$ is a unit vector pointing from object 1 to object 2 and $$\vec{F}_{12}$$ is the force object 1 exerts on object 2 — the minus sign makes the force attractive.

The Earth and the moon are separated from each other in space. The Earth is much more massive than the moon (about $$81$$ times the mass). Five points on the line through their centers are marked $$A$$ through $$E$$ below. At which marked point, if any, could an object feel zero net gravitational force from the Earth and the moon? (Ignore the sun, the galaxy, and everything else.) Answer without computing anything — reason from the directions and relative strengths of the two pulls.
answer: Point $$D$$ — between the two bodies, on the moon's side.
solution:
First, the point must lie __between__ the Earth and the moon, like $$B,$$ $$C,$$ or $$D.$$ Only there do the two pulls point in opposite directions and have a chance to cancel. At $$A$$ (beyond the Earth) and $$E$$ (beyond the moon), both bodies pull the object the same way, so the forces add instead of canceling.

Second, the point must be __closer to the moon__ than to the Earth. The moon has much less mass, so at any fixed distance its pull is weaker; to make the two pulls equal, we must shrink the distance to the moon and grow the distance to the Earth. At $$B$$ and $$C$$ (the midpoint), the Earth is both more massive and at least as close, so the Earth's pull wins. The only point that could work is $$D.$$

title: Gravity at a Small Height Above the Earth
statement:
Assume the Earth is a uniform sphere of radius $$R,$$ and let $$g_0$$ be the gravitational free-fall acceleration at its surface. What is the approximate free-fall acceleration $$g$$ at a height $$h \ll R$$ above the surface? (A) $$g = g_0$$ — there is no variation; (B) $$g \approx g_0\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)$$; (C) $$g \approx g_0\left(1 - \dfrac{h}{R}\right)$$; (D) $$g \approx g_0\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)$$; (E) $$g \approx g_0\left(1 - \dfrac{3h}{R}\right).$$

You will need Newton's gravitational law, $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2},$$ where $$r$$ is the distance measured from the __center__ of the Earth, and the approximation $$\dfrac{1}{1+\epsilon} \approx 1 - \epsilon$$ for small $$\epsilon.$$

__(a)__ Without any algebra, which answer choices can you eliminate immediately, and why?

__(b)__ Write $$g_0$$ in terms of $$G,$$ the Earth's mass $$M,$$ and $$R.$$ Then write the exact expression for $$g$$ at height $$h.$$ (Keep the three lengths straight: $$R$$ is the Earth's radius, $$h$$ is the height above the surface, and the distance from the center is $$r = R + h.$$)

__(c)__ Factor your expression so it reads $$g = g_0\cdot(\text{something}),$$ decide which term is small enough to drop, apply the approximation, and choose the answer.

__(d)__ Suppose you didn't know the approximation formula but had a calculator. How could you check the answer numerically?
solution:
__(a)__ As we move up from the surface, the distance $$r$$ in Newton's gravitational law increases, so gravity must get __weaker__. Choices (A) and (B) show $$g$$ staying constant or increasing with $$h,$$ so both are eliminated.

__(b)__ At the surface, $$h = 0$$ and $$r = R.$$ The force on a mass $$m$$ is $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{R^2},$$ and Newton's second law gives $$mg_0 = \dfrac{GMm}{R^2},$$ so $$g_0 = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}.$$ At height $$h,$$ the only change is the distance: $$g = \dfrac{GM}{(R+h)^2} = \dfrac{GM}{R^2 + 2Rh + h^2}.$$

__(c)__ Factor $$R^2$$ out of the denominator: $$g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1 + \dfrac{2h}{R} + \dfrac{h^2}{R^2}} = g_0\,\dfrac{1}{1 + \dfrac{2h}{R} + \dfrac{h^2}{R^2}}.$$ Since $$h \ll R,$$ the term $$\dfrac{h^2}{R^2}$$ is tiny compared with the other terms in the denominator (note we can __not__ drop the $$1$$ — it is the biggest term!), leaving $$g \approx g_0\,\dfrac{1}{1 + \dfrac{2h}{R}}.$$ Applying $$\dfrac{1}{1+\epsilon} \approx 1 - \epsilon$$ with $$\epsilon = \dfrac{2h}{R}$$ gives $$g \approx g_0\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right),$$ choice (D).

__(d)__ Pick a small test value such as $$\dfrac{h}{R} = 0.001.$$ Then the exact factor is $$\dfrac{1}{(1.001)^2} \approx 0.998003,$$ while choice (D) predicts $$1 - 2(0.001) = 0.998$$ — an excellent match. Choices (C) and (E) predict $$0.999$$ and $$0.997,$$ which are clearly worse.

title: Spy Satellites in Geosynchronous Orbit
statement:
__(a)__ A satellite of mass $$m$$ moves in a circular orbit of radius $$r$$ around a body of mass $$M.$$ Combine Newton's gravitational law, $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2},$$ with the circular-motion acceleration $$a = \omega^2 r$$ to find the orbit's angular frequency $$\omega$$ in terms of $$G,$$ $$M,$$ and $$r.$$ Then show that the orbital period $$T$$ satisfies $$T^2 \propto r^3.$$ (This is __Kepler's third law__.)

__(b)__ Spy satellites have been placed in the geosynchronous orbit above the Earth's equator. (__Geosynchronous__ means the satellite stays above the same spot of the Earth's surface at all times, so its period is about $$24$$ hours.) A satellite in a circular orbit just above the Earth's surface has a period of $$90$$ minutes. Use Kepler's third law to find the radius $$R'$$ of the geosynchronous orbit in terms of the Earth's radius $$R.$$

__(c)__ Using the figure below, find the greatest latitude $$L$$ from which the geosynchronous satellites are visible from the Earth's surface. The gray parts of the Earth in the figure are the regions from which the satellite cannot be seen. (Problem and figure from Halliday, Resnick, and Krane, __Physics__, 5th ed.)
solution:
__(a)__ Newton's second law for the circular orbit reads $$\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = m\omega^2 r.$$ Solving, $$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r^3}} = \sqrt{GM}\,r^{-3/2}.$$ The period is $$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} \propto r^{3/2},$$ and squaring gives $$T^2 \propto r^3.$$

__(b)__ Kepler's third law as a ratio between the two orbits: $$\dfrac{(T')^2}{T^2} = \dfrac{(R')^3}{R^3}.$$ The period ratio is $$\dfrac{24\;\mathrm{h}}{90\;\mathrm{min}} = 16,$$ so $$\dfrac{(R')^3}{R^3} = 16^2 = 256$$ and $$R' = \sqrt[3]{256}\,R = 4\cdot 2^{2/3} R \approx 6.3R.$$ (The near-surface orbit has radius essentially equal to the Earth's radius $$R.$$)

__(c)__ The extreme observer sees the satellite right on the horizon, so the line of sight from the observer to the satellite is tangent to the Earth — perpendicular to the Earth's radius at the observer. That makes a right triangle whose hypotenuse runs from the Earth's center to the satellite (length $$6.3R$$) and whose short leg is the Earth's radius to the observer (length $$R$$), with the latitude $$L$$ as the angle at the Earth's center. Then $$\cos L = \dfrac{R}{6.3R},$$ so $$L = \arccos\left(\dfrac{1}{6.3}\right) \approx 81^\circ.$$

title: Timing a Hohmann Transfer
statement:
A __Hohmann transfer orbit__ moves a rocket between two circular orbits around the sun in several steps. (1) The rocket begins in a circular orbit of radius $$r_1.$$ (2) The rocket briefly fires its engines until its orbit is an ellipse whose farthest point is a distance $$r_3$$ from the sun. (3) The rocket coasts until it is a distance $$r_3$$ from the sun, then briefly fires its engines again until it enters a circular orbit of radius $$r_3.$$ The figure shows the initial orbit (1), the transfer ellipse (2), and the final orbit (3).

Some facts about orbits, all of which follow from Newton's laws: orbits are ellipses with the sun at one focus (__Kepler's first law__). The __semi-major axis__ $$a$$ of an ellipse is half its long axis. __Kepler's third law__, $$T^2 \propto a^3,$$ holds for elliptical orbits with the semi-major axis $$a$$ in place of the circle's radius, so the period of an orbit depends only on the mass being orbited and on $$a$$ — orbits with the same semi-major axis have the same period regardless of shape. Finally, the total energy of an orbit is $$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a},$$ so a larger semi-major axis means a higher energy.

__(a)__ At each of the two engine firings, does the rocket speed up or slow down?

__(b)__ Find the semi-major axis of the transfer ellipse in terms of $$r_1$$ and $$r_3.$$

__(c)__ If the period of the original circular orbit is $$T,$$ how long does step (2) — the trip along the transfer ellipse from distance $$r_1$$ to distance $$r_3$$ — take, in terms of $$T,$$ $$r_1,$$ and $$r_3?$$
solution:
__(a)__ It speeds up both times. Each burn increases the orbit's semi-major axis: from $$r_1$$ (the circle) to $$\dfrac{r_1+r_3}{2}$$ (the transfer ellipse) to $$r_3$$ (the final circle). Since $$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a},$$ a larger semi-major axis means a higher total energy, and at the moment of a burn the position (and hence the potential energy) doesn't change — so the kinetic energy must jump up. The rocket speeds up at each firing.

__(b)__ The long axis of the transfer ellipse runs from the near point, a distance $$r_1$$ from the sun on one side, straight through the sun's side of the ellipse to the far point, a distance $$r_3$$ on the other side. So the major axis has length $$r_1 + r_3,$$ and the semi-major axis is $$a = \dfrac{r_1+r_3}{2}.$$

__(c)__ By Kepler's third law, $$T \propto a^{3/2},$$ so the full period of the transfer ellipse is $$T\left(\dfrac{(r_1+r_3)/2}{r_1}\right)^{3/2},$$ comparing its semi-major axis with the original circle's radius $$r_1.$$ The transfer covers only half the ellipse — from the near point to the far point — so the time is half a period: $$t_{\mathrm{transfer}} = \dfrac{T}{2}\left(\dfrac{(r_1+r_3)/2}{r_1}\right)^{3/2}.$$

title: Kepler's Laws with Inverse-Cube Gravity
statement:
Kepler's laws state that: (I) the orbits of planets are elliptical with one focus at the sun; (II) a line connecting the sun and a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times; and (III) the square of the period of a planet's orbit is proportional to the cube of its semi-major axis. Which of these laws would remain true if the force of gravity were proportional to $$1/r^3$$ rather than $$1/r^2?$$ (From the F=ma exam.)

The animation below illustrates Kepler's second law: a planet moves faster when it is near the sun, in just such a way that the line from the sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times. (Animation by Gonfer, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

__(a)__ First, connect Kepler's second law to a conservation law. In a short time $$\Delta t,$$ a planet at distance $$r$$ from the sun, moving at speed $$v$$ with angle $$\theta$$ between its velocity and the line to the sun, sweeps out the thin shaded triangle below. Show that the swept area is $$A = \dfrac12\,v\Delta t\cdot r\sin\theta,$$ and that $$\dfrac{2m}{\Delta t}\cdot A$$ equals the magnitude of the planet's angular momentum $$L = |\vec{r}\times\vec{p}|.$$ Conclude that Kepler's second law is equivalent to conservation of angular momentum.

__(b)__ Using part (a), decide whether law II would survive the modified force. (A force that always points along the line toward the sun is called a __central force__.)

__(c)__ For a circular orbit under the modified force $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^3},$$ redo the usual period derivation (set the force equal to $$m\omega^2 r$$) and find the exponent $$\gamma$$ in $$T \propto r^{\gamma}.$$ Does law III survive?

__(d)__ For law I, you need a fact that is hard to prove: __Bertrand's theorem__ says that orbits are ellipses only for special force laws — for $$F \propto 1/r^2$$ the orbits are ellipses with the sun at one focus, and for $$F \propto r$$ (Hooke's law) they are ellipses with the sun at the center; for other force laws, orbits do not have simple closed shapes at all. Does law I survive? State the final answer to the question.
answer: Only law II would remain true. In part (c), $$\gamma = 2$$ instead of $$3/2.$$
solution:
__(a)__ For small $$\Delta t$$ the swept region is essentially a triangle with base $$v\Delta t$$ (the planet's displacement) and height $$r\sin\theta$$ (the perpendicular distance from the sun to the line of motion), so $$A = \dfrac12\,v\Delta t\cdot r\sin\theta.$$ Multiplying by the fixed quantity $$\dfrac{2m}{\Delta t}$$ gives $$\dfrac{2m}{\Delta t}\cdot A = mvr\sin\theta = |\vec{r}||\vec{p}|\sin\theta = |\vec{r}\times\vec{p}| = L.$$ So the rate of sweeping area is $$\dfrac{A}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{L}{2m}$$: the sweep rate is constant exactly when the angular momentum is constant. Kepler's second law is conservation of angular momentum in disguise.

__(b)__ Law II survives. An inverse-cube force still points along the line from the planet to the sun, so it exerts no torque about the sun, and the planet's angular momentum about the sun is still conserved. By part (a), equal areas are still swept in equal times. This holds for __any__ central force, no matter its dependence on distance.

__(c)__ Newton's second law for a circular orbit now reads $$\dfrac{GMm}{r^3} = m\omega^2 r.$$ Ignoring the constants $$G$$ and $$M$$ (we only want the scaling), $$\omega^2 \propto r^{-4},$$ so $$\omega \propto r^{-2}$$ and $$T \propto r^{2}.$$ The exponent is $$\gamma = 2,$$ not $$\dfrac32,$$ so law III fails.

__(d)__ By Bertrand's theorem, $$1/r^3$$ is not one of the special force laws that produce elliptical orbits, so law I fails as well. The final answer: only Kepler's second law would remain true.

title: Gravitational Potential Energy and a Two-Particle Escape
statement:
__(a)__ The gravitational potential energy of a system of two particles with masses $$m_1$$ and $$m_2$$ separated by a distance $$r$$ has the form $$U = -\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^n}$$ for some number $$n.$$ Use __dimensional analysis__ to find $$n.$$ (Two useful facts: the gravitational force is $$F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2},$$ and the work-energy theorem $$W = F\Delta x$$ shows that a force times a distance is an energy.)

__(b)__ Dimensional analysis cannot determine the sign or the overall numerical constant. Explain why the formula must carry a minus sign, $$U = -\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r},$$ rather than being $$+\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r}.$$ (Think about whether the potential energy should rise or fall as the particles move farther apart.)

__(c)__ Two point-like particles, each of mass $$m,$$ are originally separated by a distance $$d$$ and are moving in opposite directions along the line joining them, each with speed $$v.$$ What is the maximum value of $$v$$ so that the particles will eventually move back together under their mutual gravitational attraction? (Hint: forces are awkward here, because the force keeps changing as the separation changes — use conservation of energy. Note that $$d$$ is the distance __between__ the particles, so the system's potential energy is $$-\dfrac{Gm^2}{d},$$ not $$-\dfrac{Gm^2}{2d}.)$$

__(d)__ A gravitational system with total energy $$E < 0$$ is called __bound__: the bodies cannot escape each other. A system with $$E > 0$$ is called __free__: the bodies escape forever. If the two particles in part (c) are launched slightly faster than the maximum speed you found, are they bound or free? Also state which conic-section path a small body near a star follows in the cases $$E < 0,$$ $$E = 0,$$ and $$E > 0.$$
answer: (a) $$n = 1$$; (c) $$v_{\max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{Gm}{d}}$$ (the escape velocity); (d) free; ellipse, parabola, hyperbola respectively
solution:
__(a)__ The combination $$\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$$ has dimensions of force, and force times distance is energy. Multiplying by the only available distance, $$r,$$ gives $$\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}\cdot r = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r},$$ which has dimensions of energy. So $$n = 1.$$ (Dimensional analysis can't rule out an extra dimensionless coefficient, but this is the best we can do without calculus — and the coefficient does turn out to be $$1.)$$

__(b)__ To pull the particles farther apart, we must do positive work against their gravitational attraction, so the potential energy must __increase__ with separation. The function $$-\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r}$$ increases (from very negative toward zero) as $$r$$ grows, while $$+\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r}$$ decreases. So the minus sign is required: $$U = -\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r},$$ with $$U \to 0$$ as $$r \to \infty.$$

__(c)__ The total energy is conserved: $$E = 2\cdot\dfrac12 mv^2 - \dfrac{Gm^2}{d} = mv^2 - \dfrac{Gm^2}{d}.$$ At the maximum speed, the particles are exactly at the threshold between returning and escaping: they drift apart forever, coming to rest essentially infinitely far from each other. Far apart, the potential energy goes to zero (it is proportional to $$1/r)$$ and the kinetic energy goes to zero, so the total energy is zero. Setting $$E = 0$$ gives $$mv^2 = \dfrac{Gm^2}{d},$$ so $$v_{\max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{Gm}{d}}.$$ A speed like this — the largest speed that still falls back, or equivalently the smallest speed that escapes — is called the __escape velocity__.

__(d)__ Slightly faster than $$v_{\max}$$ means $$E > 0,$$ so the system is free: the particles separate forever, still moving when they are far apart. For a small body near a star, the path is an ellipse if $$E < 0,$$ a parabola if $$E = 0,$$ and a hyperbola if $$E > 0.$$ (The parabola and hyperbola are not closed orbits — the body drifts away and never returns.)

title: The Energy of an Orbit, and Comparing Orbits
statement:
__(a)__ A planet of mass $$m$$ orbits a star of mass $$M$$ in a circular orbit of radius $$R.$$ Find the planet's kinetic energy, the system's gravitational potential energy (use $$U = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}),$$ and the total energy, in terms of $$G,$$ $$M,$$ $$m,$$ and $$R.$$ (Hint: the planet's acceleration is both $$\dfrac{v^2}{R}$$ from circular motion and $$\dfrac{GM}{R^2}$$ from gravity; use that to eliminate $$v.)$$

__(b)__ Check that your answers satisfy $$KE = -\dfrac12 U.$$ This is a special case of the __virial theorem__: for any orbit, the kinetic energy averaged over a full orbit is $$-\dfrac12$$ times the averaged potential energy (for a circular orbit it holds at every instant). A second general fact: the total energy of any elliptical orbit is $$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a},$$ where $$a$$ is the semi-major axis — your circular-orbit answer is the special case $$a = R.$$

Now use these tools on a classic comparison problem. The figure below (from Halliday, Resnick, and Krane, __Physics__, 5th ed.) shows several possible orbits of a satellite around the sun: two circular orbits — the larger circle $$A$$ and the smaller circle $$D$$ — and two elliptical orbits $$B$$ and $$C$$ whose farthest points lie on circle $$A.$$ Orbit $$C$$'s closest approach to the sun is at the radius of circle $$D,$$ while orbit $$B$$ passes much closer to the sun. For each part, give the answer and the reasoning.

__(c)__ Which orbit has the largest angular momentum? (Useful facts: the rate at which an orbit sweeps out area is $$\dfrac{A}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{L}{2m},$$ so comparing angular momenta is the same as comparing sweep rates; for a circular orbit the sweep rate is $$\dfrac12 vr$$; and combining Kepler's third law $$\omega \propto r^{-3/2}$$ with $$v = \omega r$$ gives $$v \propto r^{-1/2}$$ for circular orbits.)

__(d)__ Which orbit has the largest total energy?

__(e)__ On which orbit does the satellite reach the largest speed?
solution:
__(a)__ Equating the two expressions for the acceleration, $$\dfrac{v^2}{R} = \dfrac{GM}{R^2},$$ gives $$v^2 = \dfrac{GM}{R}.$$ Then $$KE = \dfrac12 mv^2 = \dfrac{GMm}{2R}.$$ The potential energy is $$U = -\dfrac{GMm}{R},$$ so the total energy is $$E = KE + U = -\dfrac{GMm}{2R}.$$

__(b)__ Indeed $$\dfrac{GMm}{2R} = -\dfrac12\left(-\dfrac{GMm}{R}\right),$$ confirming the virial relation, and $$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2R}$$ matches $$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a}$$ with $$a = R.$$ The kinetic energy in a circular orbit is exactly half of what would be needed to escape.

__(c)__ Compare the circles first: the sweep rate is $$\dfrac12 vr \propto r^{-1/2}\cdot r = r^{1/2},$$ so the larger circle $$A$$ sweeps out more area per unit time than $$D$$ — the longer arm beats the higher speed. Now compare $$A$$ with the ellipses at the leftmost point of $$C,$$ where $$C$$ touches circle $$A$$: there the satellite on orbit $$C$$ is at its farthest point and starts falling back toward the sun, so it is moving too slowly to stay in a circular orbit at that radius — slower than a satellite on $$A$$ at the same spot. Same arm length, smaller speed, smaller sweep rate. The same logic applies to $$B.$$ So orbit $$A$$ has the largest angular momentum.

__(d)__ The total energy is $$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a},$$ which increases as the semi-major axis $$a$$ increases. Orbit $$A$$ has the largest semi-major axis ($$B,$$ $$C,$$ and $$D$$ all fit inside it with shorter semi-major axes), so $$A$$ has the largest total energy.

__(e)__ By energy conservation, the fastest point of any orbit is its closest approach to the sun. Among the circles, the smaller one is faster: $$v \propto r^{-1/2},$$ so $$D$$ beats $$A.$$ Comparing $$D$$ and $$C$$: at $$C$$'s closest approach it is at the same distance from the sun as $$D,$$ but it has too much speed to stay in a circular orbit there — that's why it climbs out to the radius of $$A$$ — so $$C$$'s top speed beats $$D$$'s. Finally, $$B$$ dives much closer to the sun than $$C$$ does; near its closest approach the potential energy $$U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$$ becomes very negative, so by energy conservation the kinetic energy becomes very large. The closer the near side of an orbit gets to the sun (with a fixed far side), the faster its fastest point. Orbit $$B$$ reaches the largest speed.

title: Gravity Inside and Outside a Uniform Planet
statement:
The __shell theorem__, proved by Newton, has two parts. First: the gravitational pull of any spherically symmetric body, felt from outside the body, is exactly the same as if all of its mass were concentrated at its center. (This is why we can use the Earth's radius as the distance $$r$$ in $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$$ when standing on the surface, even though some of the Earth is just beneath our feet and some is a full diameter away — the averaging over the whole sphere works out perfectly. It holds even for spheres that are denser in the middle, like the Earth and the sun.) Second: a spherically symmetric __shell__ of mass exerts no net gravitational force at all on an object anywhere inside it.

A certain planet is a uniform sphere of radius $$R$$ and density $$\rho,$$ so its total mass is $$M = \dfrac43\pi R^3\rho.$$ Sketch a plot of the gravitational acceleration $$g$$ due to the planet as a function of the distance $$r$$ from the planet's center, from $$r = 0$$ out to several times $$R.$$ Proceed in stages:

__(a)__ Find $$g(r)$$ for points outside the planet, $$r > R.$$

__(b)__ For a point inside the planet at radius $$r < R,$$ divide the planet's mass into the part closer to the center than $$r$$ (the shaded sphere in the figure) and the part farther from the center (the surrounding shell). How much mass is in the inner part, in terms of $$M,$$ $$r,$$ and $$R,$$ and how much does each part contribute to the gravitational acceleration at radius $$r?$$

__(c)__ Find $$g(r)$$ for $$r < R,$$ then describe the complete plot: the shape of the curve on each side of $$r = R,$$ the value $$g_s$$ of the acceleration at the surface, and what happens at $$r = R.$$
answer: $$g = \dfrac{GMr}{R^3}$$ (a straight line) for $$r < R$$ and $$g = \dfrac{GM}{r^2}$$ for $$r > R$$; the plot peaks at the surface value $$g_s = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$$ at $$r = R.$$
solution:
__(a)__ By the first shell theorem, from outside the planet we may treat all of its mass as sitting at the center. The force on a test mass $$m$$ is $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2},$$ so the acceleration is $$g = \dfrac{GM}{r^2}$$ for $$r > R.$$

__(b)__ The inner sphere of radius $$r$$ has mass $$M_{\mathrm{closer}} = \dfrac43\pi\rho r^3 = M\left(\dfrac{r}{R}\right)^3,$$ using $$M = \dfrac43\pi\rho R^3.$$ By the first shell theorem it pulls like a point mass at the center. The outer part is a collection of spherical shells that the point at radius $$r$$ sits __inside__, so by the second shell theorem it contributes nothing at all.

__(c)__ Only the inner mass counts: $$g = \dfrac{GM_{\mathrm{closer}}}{r^2} = \dfrac{GM r}{R^3}$$ for $$r < R$$ — a straight line through the origin. This makes sense: the enclosed mass grows like $$r^3$$ while the $$1/r^2$$ factor shrinks, leaving a net factor of $$r.$$ Outside, $$g = \dfrac{GM}{r^2}$$ decreases toward zero. The two pieces meet at the surface, where $$g_s = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$$ — the maximum of the whole plot — with a kink at $$r = R$$:
